h1: Calculate Your Ideal Water Heater Tank Size
description: Find the right water heater tank size (liters or gallons) for your household. Enter number of people and daily usage intensity — get an immediate, plumber-grade recommendation.
seoKeywords: hot water tank capacity per person
how many gallons water heater per person
intro:
Choosing the wrong water heater size is one of the most common — and most expensive — mistakes in home construction and renovation. Too small, and your household runs out of hot water every morning. Too large, and you pay to keep surplus water hot around the clock, inflating your energy bill for years.

The right starting point is the method licensed plumbers use: estimate how much hot water (at 60 °C / 140 °F) each person in the house consumes daily — roughly 22–42 liters (6–11 gallons) depending on bathing habits — then apply a simultaneity factor, because not everyone showers at exactly the same moment. That calculation gives your peak demand, which you round up to the nearest commercially available tank size.

This calculator applies that same logic. Enter your household size, daily usage intensity (low / average / high), and whether you want a storage tank or an instant (tankless) heater. You get an immediate, specific recommendation — including the size in liters, estimated daily demand, the simultaneity factor used, and a note on commercial models.
keyTakeaway: **Peak demand = people × liters/person × simultaneity factor**. Standard storage sizes: 50 L (1-2 people) · 80 L (2-3) · 120 L (4-5) · 150 L (6) · 180+ L (7+). If two showers run simultaneously, go one size up.

explanation:
## How It's Calculated

Water heater sizing follows a two-step method used by licensed plumbers and aligned with the U.S. DOE Energy Saver guidelines and Argentine ENARGAS standards:

```
Step 1 — Daily demand
  Demand = people × liters per person per day (at 60 °C / 140 °F)
       Low usage    → 22 L/person   (~6 gal)
       Average      → 30 L/person   (~8 gal)  ← standard reference
       High usage   → 42 L/person   (~11 gal)

Step 2 — Peak simultaneity factor
  1-2 people  → × 1.00 (full overlap possible)
  3-4 people  → × 0.85
  5-6 people  → × 0.75
  7+ people   → × 0.65

Peak demand = Step 1 × Step 2
Round UP to the next standard commercial tank size.
```

**Standard commercial storage sizes**: 50 · 80 · 120 · 150 · 180 · 200 L (13 · 21 · 32 · 40 · 48 · 53 gal)

For **tankless (on-demand) heaters**, the metric is flow rate in L/min (or GPM):
- 1-2 people: **14 L/min** (~3.7 GPM) — covers one shower at a time
- 3-4 people: **22 L/min** (~5.8 GPM, modulating) — handles two simultaneous showers
- 5+ people: 22 L/min + auxiliary storage, or two separate units

## Storage Tank vs. Tankless — Quick Comparison

| | Tankless 14 L/min | Tankless 22 L/min | Storage tank |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Simultaneous showers** | 1 | 2 | 2-3 (size-dependent) |
| **Standby heat loss** | None | None | 10-15% of daily energy |
| **Hot water wait** | Instant | Instant | 10-60 s pipe purge |
| **Best for** | 1-2 people, 1 bath | 2-4 people, 2 baths | Families of 3+ |

## Common Sizing Mistakes

- **Buying by physical size**: a horizontal 80 L tank and a vertical 80 L tank hold the same amount. Always check the nominal liters on the spec sheet.
- **Ignoring recovery rate**: an 80 L tank with a fast-recovery burner (20 min) outperforms a 120 L slow-recovery unit (90 min) for back-to-back showers. Check kW or BTU input alongside tank volume.
- **Choosing tankless for two simultaneous showers at 14 L/min**: two showers consume roughly 18-20 L/min combined. A 14 L/min unit can't keep up. Use 22 L/min or a storage tank.
- **Skipping anode rod replacement**: this sacrificial magnesium rod prevents tank corrosion and should be inspected every 2-3 years and replaced when more than 50% depleted.

faq.q: How many liters or gallons of hot water does the average person use per day?
faq.a: The standard reference for sizing purposes is **30 liters (8 gallons) of hot water at 60 °C per person per day** for average household use. This accounts for one standard 10-minute shower, hand washing, and a share of dishwasher and laundry use. Short-shower households may only need 22 L/person; households with bathtubs, long showers, or hot-water washing machines may need up to 42 L/person. This calculator lets you select your actual usage intensity to get a more accurate result.

faq.q: What is 'first-hour rating' (FHR) and why does it matter?
faq.a: First-hour rating (FHR) is the volume of hot water a storage tank can deliver in the first hour of operation starting from a full, hot tank. It equals roughly 70% of tank volume plus the hourly recovery volume (how fast the burner or element can reheat). A 50-gallon gas heater with 40 GPH recovery delivers FHR ≈ 75 gallons — more usable capacity than its nominal volume. The U.S. DOE requires FHR to appear on the EnergyGuide label. **When comparing storage tanks, match FHR to your peak-hour demand**, not just tank volume.

faq.q: Does the fuel type (gas, electric, heat pump) change the size I need?
faq.a: Yes. **Gas heaters recover faster** (30-50 gallons/hour) than standard electric resistance heaters (18-25 gallons/hour), so a 40-gallon gas unit often delivers the same usable hot water per hour as a 50-gallon electric unit. **Heat pump water heaters** are very efficient but recover slowly, so they benefit from a larger tank to buffer demand. If switching fuel types during a replacement, don't assume a same-volume swap — recalculate based on first-hour rating.

faq.q: Should I buy one size larger 'just to be safe'?
faq.a: Oversizing has real, ongoing costs: every extra liter stored at 60 °C loses heat to the surroundings 24/7 — standby loss adds $30-80/year per extra 20 gallons, depending on insulation and fuel cost. Undersizing is usually worse (cold showers, constant cycling, shortened element life), but reflexive oversizing wastes money too. The right approach: use accurate sizing with a one-step-up buffer only when you're between sizes — exactly what this calculator's simultaneity factor provides.

faq.q: How does cold inlet water temperature affect sizing?
faq.a: The colder the incoming groundwater, the more energy the heater needs per liter and the slower the recovery. In cold-climate regions (northern U.S., Canada, Patagonia), groundwater may enter at 4-8 °C in winter, effectively reducing first-hour capacity compared to warmer regions where groundwater enters at 16-20 °C. If you live in a cold climate and your usage falls at the upper end of a size range, choose the next tank size up or select a unit with higher BTU/kW input.

faq.q: What's the difference between storage tank and tankless (on-demand) heaters for sizing?
faq.a: **Storage tanks** are sized by volume (liters or gallons) plus recovery rate. **Tankless heaters** produce hot water continuously and are sized by flow rate (liters per minute or GPM) and temperature rise. A tankless unit never 'runs out' if properly sized — but it costs more upfront ($800-3,000+ installed vs. $500-1,500 for storage) and has higher installation complexity. Tankless units also eliminate standby heat loss entirely, which can justify the premium in low-usage single or two-person households.

faq.q: How do I manually calculate my peak-hour demand?
faq.a: List every hot water activity during your household's busiest hour (typically the morning rush). Standard amounts: shower = 10 gallons (38 L), bath = 20 gallons (76 L), shaving at sink = 2 gallons (8 L), hand washing = 1 gallon (4 L), dishwasher cycle = 6 gallons (23 L), clothes washer warm = 7 gallons (26 L). Add them up — that total is your peak-hour demand. Then choose a tank with a first-hour rating (FHR) that meets or exceeds that number.

faq.q: How long do water heaters last and when should I replace rather than repair?
faq.a: Storage tank water heaters typically last **8-12 years** with routine maintenance; tankless units can reach 15-20 years. Replace rather than repair when: the unit is over 10 years old, there is rust-colored water (internal corrosion), leaks appear at the tank base (failed inner lining — not repairable), or repair estimates exceed 50% of replacement cost. Regular maintenance — flushing sediment annually and inspecting the anode rod every 2-3 years — significantly extends tank life.

faq.q: Can this calculator be used for a rental property or small commercial building?
faq.a: This calculator is optimized for residential households of 1-10 people with standard usage patterns. For commercial applications — hotels, restaurants, laundromats, or apartment buildings — professional load calculations using ASHRAE or PHCC (Plumbing-Heating-Cooling Contractors Association) guidelines are recommended. For a vacation rental (2-3 bedrooms, up to 6 guests), selecting the high-usage setting at maximum occupancy provides a reasonable residential-grade estimate.

faq.q: What maintenance steps extend water heater life and efficiency most?
faq.a: Four tasks make the biggest difference. (1) **Flush sediment annually**: connect a hose to the drain valve, turn off the cold inlet, drain until water runs clear. Sediment insulates the heating element and raises energy use 5-10%. (2) **Inspect the anode rod every 2-3 years** — replace when more than 50% depleted. (3) **Test the temperature/pressure relief (TPR) valve annually** by briefly lifting the lever. (4) **Keep the thermostat at 60 °C (140 °F)** — higher temperatures accelerate scale and corrosion; lower temperatures risk Legionella growth.

faq.q: Are there safety or code requirements I should know before buying?
faq.a: Several. Most jurisdictions require a licensed plumber for installation and a permit with inspection — DIY installation may void the manufacturer's warranty and homeowner's insurance. The unit must include a properly sized temperature/pressure relief (TPR) valve vented close to floor level or to the exterior. Gas units need adequate combustion air and proper flue venting. In earthquake-prone regions (California, Pacific Northwest, Japan, New Zealand), seismic strapping is required by code and is good practice everywhere. Always verify local plumbing code requirements before purchasing.

faq.q: What is the energy cost impact of a correctly-sized vs. undersized water heater?
faq.a: An undersized tank runs its heating element or burner almost continuously during demand peaks, then cycles on and off throughout the day — less efficient than normal operation. When it runs out of hot water, users often take longer showers waiting for reheating, increasing total consumption. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that right-sizing alone — without any other efficiency upgrade — can reduce water heating energy use by 10-15% compared to chronic undersizing. Proper insulation, temperature settings, and annual maintenance compound those savings further.
